v.q: What does the Single Responsibility Principle say?
o: A class should have one reason to change
A class should contain only one method
A class should have only one field
A class should have only one caller
v.w: "Responsibility" means a reason to change, such as business rules versus persistence. It is not a method count.

v.q: Which class breaks the Single Responsibility Principle?
o: One that calculates fees and also sends emails
One that only validates cards
One that only formats dates
One that only stores accounts
v.w: It has two reasons to change, so each job should live in its own class.

v.q: A `ReportService` has a long `if/else` over report types and you edit it for every new type. Which principle does this violate?
o: Open-Closed: extend behaviour instead of editing existing code
Liskov Substitution
Interface Segregation
Dependency Inversion
v.w: Introduce a `ReportGenerator` interface and a class per type, for example with the Strategy pattern, so new types do not touch old code.

v.q: Which change adds a new report type without editing existing code?
o: Add a new implementation
Add another else-if
Copy the method
Add a flag to the constructor
v.w: Open-Closed: extend with new code and leave the tested code alone.

v.q: What does the Liskov Substitution Principle require?
o: A subtype must work wherever the base type is expected
A subclass must override every inherited method
A base class must always be abstract
A subtype must add more fields than its base
v.w: A subtype must not strengthen preconditions or weaken postconditions. A `ReadOnlyList` that throws on `add` breaks it.

o: One that throws for a method its parent supports
One that adds a new method
One that has a new field
One that overrides with the same behaviour
v.w: Callers using the parent type would get surprises.

v.q: An interface `Worker` has `work()`, `eat()` and `sleep()`, and a `Robot` has to implement `eat()` with an exception. Which principle is violated?
o: Interface Segregation: don't depend on methods you don't use
Single Responsibility
Open-Closed
Liskov Substitution alone
v.w: Split into smaller role interfaces such as `Workable` and `Feedable`. Classes then implement only what applies to them.

o: Split Worker into smaller interfaces
Add more methods to Worker
Make Worker a class
Throw exceptions for unused methods
v.w: Clients should depend only on the methods they use.

o: High-level code should depend on abstractions, not concrete classes
Low-level code should call high-level code directly
All dependencies should be made static
Classes should create their own dependencies
v.w: The business service depends on a `PaymentGateway` interface and the concrete implementation is supplied from outside.

o: Takes a PaymentGateway interface
Calls new StripeGateway()
Reads a static field
Uses a singleton getInstance
v.w: The class depends on an abstraction, so a test can pass a fake.

v.q: How does Spring's dependency injection support Dependency Inversion?
o: The container supplies implementations, so classes see only interfaces
It turns every bean into a static singleton in the JVM
It hides every interface from the developers who use it
It generates the business logic itself from the configuration
v.w: Constructor injection of an interface makes classes easy to test with fakes, and implementations easy to swap.

v.q: Which statement about Spring and SOLID is NOT true?
o: It forces every class to be a static singleton
It injects implementations
It helps tests use mocks
It reduces new calls in business code
v.w: Beans are configured and injected, so code depends on interfaces and not on construction details.

v.q: A `UserService` builds emails, writes to the database and formats PDF statements. What is the most sensible fix?
o: Split it into focused classes, one per reason to change
Add more methods with clearer names
Make the class final so nobody extends it
Move everything into a static utility class
v.w: Separate notification, persistence and reporting so a change in one does not risk the others.

v.q: Which refactor is best for a class with 3000 lines doing five jobs?
o: Extract focused classes
Add comments
Make methods static
Move to another package
v.w: Group code by the reason it changes, then name the classes after the job.

v.q: Is applying every SOLID principle to the extreme always good?
o: No, over-abstraction adds complexity, so apply them where change happens
Yes, because adding more interfaces is always an improvement
Yes, every single class in the codebase needs its own interface
No, because the principles only apply to Java code and nothing else
v.w: Principles are guidelines. Premature abstraction creates indirection with no benefit. Refactor when a second variation appears.

v.q: Which statement about applying SOLID is NOT true?
o: An interface for every class always improves design
Over-abstraction adds complexity
Apply it where change happens
Principles guide judgement
v.w: Abstractions cost something, so add them where variation is real.
